content: Exercise intensity refers to the amount of physical effort exerted during exercise. The level of intensity influences the type of fuel the body utilizes and determines the physiological adaptations that occur as a result of the exercise, commonly referred to as the training effect. Fuel Utilization The body relies on varying proportions of carbohydrates and fats as energy sources, depending on the intensity of the exercise and the individual's heart rate. For example, the heart rate values provided below are based on a 20-year-old individual with a maximum heart rate (MHR) of 200 beats per minute. Training Effects by Intensity Levels Low Intensity (up to 80% MHR) Engaging in low-intensity exercise primarily enhances overall fitness and improves the muscles' ability to efficiently utilize oxygen delivered through the bloodstream. This is achieved by increasing the number of capillaries within the muscle tissue, which facilitates better oxygen delivery and utilization. Medium Intensity (80-85% MHR) At this level, the exercise intensity approaches the anaerobic threshold (AT). Training at this intensity improves the individual's anaerobic threshold, enabling the body to sustain higher levels of exertion while still operating within the aerobic energy system. High Intensity (85-90% MHR) The heart, being a muscle, can be conditioned to become stronger and more efficient through high-intensity exercise. At this level, the heart is subjected to a significant workload, which strengthens it and enhances its ability to pump a greater volume of blood with each contraction. Maximum Effort or Flat Out (90-100% MHR) In this range, the body operates entirely anaerobically, leading to a rapid accumulation of lactate (commonly referred to as lactic acid). Although this type of training is highly demanding and often painful, it is effective in improving the body's anaerobic capacity. This includes enhancing the production, clearance, and tolerance of lactate during high-intensity efforts.
